parts: Like preparing a dinner (planning the menu and arranging ingredients, cooking, presenting), a television programme is made in three stages. (1) Pre-production: everything done before entering the studio or reaching the location: idea generation, research, scripting, discussions with crew and talent, arranging equipment, tapes, properties, costumes, set designing or location hunting and booking editing shifts. The most important element is a clear idea and a detailed script; planning everything in advance makes the other two stages easy. (2) Production: on the studio floor or location, when actually shooting: managing facilities, handling talent and crew, controlling the crowd, shooting without hurdles and solving problems on the spot. (3) Post-production: giving final shape: cutting visuals to length, arranging them in sequence, effects, text and captions, commentary recording, music recording and final assembly (editing).

Camera: the most basic equipment; the lens forms an optical image which the camera converts into an electrical (video) signal. Lights: give the camera adequate illumination, show viewers what objects look like (season and time of day) and establish the general mood. Microphone: converts sound waves into electrical audio signals (different types for news anchors, tennis matches, rock concerts); the signal is amplified and reconverted by a loudspeaker. Sound recorder: records the sound picked up by the microphone; can select a microphone, amplify a weak signal, control volume and quality, and mix two or more sources. Videotape recorder: visuals recorded on video tape or computer disk before telecast. Post-production editing machine: selects the relevant visuals and copies them in a specific order (editing); it cannot make creative decisions for you.

Television production is a team effort. Producer: head of the production, manages the budget, coordinates with advertising agencies, actors and writers and with technical and non-technical elements. Director: directs actors and technical operations; transforms the script into audio and video; decides camera placement, visuals and positions of actors. Production assistant: facilitates smooth execution and assists the producer and director. Script writer: writes the script (dialogues, list of actors, costumes, mood, locations). Actors perform roles. Anchor: presents a programme formally (news anchors, reality show anchors). Cameraperson (videographer): operates cameras, often lighting in small productions. Sound recordist: records the sound track (dialogue, effects) and background music. Art director: in charge of creative design aspects (set design, location and graphics). Property manager: manages sets and properties in large productions. Floor manager (floor director or stage manager): in charge of all activities on the studio floor, conveys the director's instructions and supervises floor personnel. Costume designer: designs and sometimes constructs costumes.
Studio and outdoor recording; live and recorded programmes

Studio recording is done within the four walls of a studio; outdoor recording is shooting outside it. Live programmes (cricket match, Republic Day parade) depend entirely on the performance of talent and crew, are made speedily and generate excitement; recorded programmes offer retakes, can be polished and edited and have a better chance of marketing but lack the excitement. Pre-production research and paper work is a must for both.
